title: Cap. VIII Arg.: peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum — therefore also of reprobation
latin: Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis ipsius: Ergo etiam reprobationis Divinae, ut respicit illos effectus. Quod enim attinet ad primum effectum, scilicet indurationem seu subtractionem peculiaris gratiae, patet illam ex peccatorum antecedentium demeritis oriri: Rom. i.; 2 Thess. ii.; Exod. ix. Quod attinet ad ultimum effectum, nempe aeternam damnationem, patet ejus causam esse demerita humana ex ipsa forma sententiae latae in judicio finali.
pass_a: The sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation itself: Therefore also of Divine reprobation, as it regards those effects. For as to what pertains to the first effect, namely hardening or the subtraction of peculiar grace, it is plain that it arises from the demerits of antecedent sins: Rom. 1; 2 Thess. 2; Exod. 9. As to what pertains to the last effect, namely eternal damnation, it is plain that its cause is human demerits from the very form of the sentence passed in the final judgment.
pass_b: Argument: the sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation itself; therefore also of divine reprobation as it regards those effects. As to the first effect — hardening or subtraction of peculiar grace — it plainly arises from demerits of antecedent sins (Rom. 1; 2 Thess. 2; Exod. 9). As to the last — eternal damnation — human demerits are plainly its cause from the very form of the sentence passed at the final judgment.

lemmas.gloss: sins cause all effects of reprobation
first and last effects cited from Scripture

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: if reprobation means damnation we grant; negative reprobation is antecedent, not damnation
latin: Non negamus peccata impiorum esse causam damnationis eorundem: et si adversarii, qui contendunt causam motivam reprobationis esse peccata quibus reprobi praevidentur vitam finituri, per reprobationem intelligant nihil aliud quam damnationem sive propositum damnandi, eatenus illis adstipulamur. Verum de reprobatione negativa disputamus, quae non est ipsa damnatio, nec causa damnationis, sed quoddam antecedens. Nemo enim damnatur quia reprobatus, sed quia reus: neque mors aeterna stipendium est reprobationis, sed transgressionis. Missa igitur damnatione, quae satis improprie dicitur effectus hujus reprobationis, de reliquis videamus.
pass_a: We do not deny that the sins of the ungodly are the cause of the damnation of the same: and if the adversaries, who contend that the moving cause of reprobation is the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as about to finish life, understand by reprobation nothing other than damnation or the purpose of damning, so far we agree with them. But we dispute concerning negative reprobation, which is not damnation itself, nor the cause of damnation, but a certain antecedent. For no one is damned because he is reprobated, but because he is guilty: nor is eternal death the wage of reprobation, but of transgression. Damnation therefore being dismissed, which is sufficiently improperly called an effect of this reprobation, let us see concerning the rest.
pass_b: We do not deny that the ungodly's sins cause their damnation. If adversaries, who make the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as finishing life the moving cause of reprobation, mean by reprobation nothing but damnation or the purpose to damn, so far we agree. But we are disputing negative reprobation — which is not damnation itself, nor damnation's cause, but a certain antecedent. No one is damned because reprobated, but because guilty; eternal death is the wage of transgression, not of reprobation. Set damnation aside, then — it is only improperly called an effect of this reprobation — and let us look at the rest.

lemmas.gloss: eternal death wages sin, not reprobation

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo: slippery consequence — cause of the permitted thing is not cause of the permission
latin: Primo, quod arguitur, Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis: Ergo etiam et ipsius rei, scilicet reprobationis Divinae, ut respicit illos effectus, haec prorsus consequentia lubrica est et infirma, si ea omnia mala vocentur effecta quae eam consequuntur. Nam illud potest esse causa rei permissae quod non sit causa permissionis relatae ad rem permissam. Verbi gratia, video duos ebrios homines temere hac illuc errantes; praevideo utrumque in foveam lapsurum, et fame ibi periturum, nisi inde illis prospiciatur. Decerno apud animum alterum eorum monere, retrahere, et ab hoc periculo efficaciter liberare; alterum non monere, non retrahere; aut saltem non ita monere et retrahere ut de facto liberetur. Decidit jam iste posterior in foveam, ibi diu jacet, maceratur, et tandem fame exstinguitur.
pass_a: First, what is argued, The sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation: Therefore also of the thing itself, namely of Divine reprobation, as it regards those effects, this consequence is altogether slippery and weak, if all those evils be called effects which follow it. For that can be the cause of the permitted thing which is not the cause of the permission related to the permitted thing. For example, I see two drunken men rashly wandering hither and thither; I foresee that both will fall into a pit, and there perish by hunger, unless provision be made for them thence. I decree in my mind to warn one of them, to draw him back, and efficaciously to free him from this peril; the other not to warn, not to draw back; or at least not so to warn and draw back that in fact he be freed. Now that latter has fallen into the pit, there he lies long, is wasted, and at length is extinguished by hunger.
pass_b: First: the argument — sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore also divine reprobation itself as regards those effects — is a slippery, weak consequence if every evil that follows is called an effect. What causes the permitted thing need not cause the permission of that thing. Example: I see two drunken men wandering rashly about; I foresee both will fall into a pit and starve there unless helped. I resolve to warn one, draw him back, and free him from the peril; the other I will not warn or draw back — or at least not so as actually to free him. That latter falls into the pit, lies long, wastes, and at last starves.

lemmas.gloss: pit analogy: cause of fall ≠ cause of leaving him

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo cont.: cause of rebellion is corrupt nature; cause of permitting decree is free pleasure
latin: Jam si quaeratur causa mali permissi in omnibus et singulis hisce effectis, scilicet in ipsa praecipitatione, in diuturna illa maceratione, in denique ipsa postrema exstinctione, recte omnium causam veredixerim fuisse praedictae personae ebrietatem, caecitatem ac temeritatem. At si quaeratur causa permissionis meae sive decreti mei permittentis de eodem homine non efficaciter liberando, hic ad liberam voluntatis meae potentiam, non ad illius inscitiam aut temeritatem, est deveniendum. Sic Deus intuetur omnes homines orbitate caecos et in peccati via errantes: quibusdam praeparat efficacem gratiam, qua quasi crapulam discutiant, ad se redeant, et serventur; statuit etiam e contra, alios hac tam potente peculiari et efficaci gratia non juvare. Hi posteriores ruunt in foedas concupiscentias, peccatum addunt peccato, in peccatis obdurantur, obduratique moriuntur, et damnantur. Si quaeratur causa rebellionis, obdurationis, perditionis quoad tales, vere respondere possumus, corruptam illorum naturam et peccata voluntaria horum omnium malorum fuisse causam et originem: At si quaeratur causa decreti permittentis quoad haec omnia, ad voluntatis Divinae liberrimum placitum, non ad ipsa peccata permissa, est deveniendum. Vacillat ergo illa consequentia, Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis: Ergo etiam sunt causa reprobationis ipsius, sive decreti reprobantis.
pass_a: Now if the cause of the permitted evil be asked in all and singular these effects, namely in the very falling headlong, in that long wasting, finally in the very last extinction, I would rightly have said that the cause of all was the drunkenness, blindness, and rashness of the foresaid person. But if the cause of my permission or of my permitting decree concerning the same man not being efficaciously freed be asked, here one must come unto the free power of my will, not unto his ignorance or rashness. So God regards all men blind by orphanhood and wandering in the way of sin: for certain ones he prepares efficacious grace, by which as it were they shake off drunkenness, return unto themselves, and are saved; he also decrees on the contrary not to help others with this so powerful peculiar and efficacious grace. These latter rush into foul lusts, add sin to sin, are hardened in sins, and hardened die, and are damned. If the cause of rebellion, hardening, perdition as to such be asked, we can truly answer that their corrupt nature and voluntary sins were the cause and origin of all these evils: But if the cause of the permitting decree as to all these be asked, one must come unto the freest pleasure of the Divine will, not unto the permitted sins themselves. That consequence therefore wavers, The sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation: Therefore they are also the cause of reprobation itself, or of the reprobating decree.
pass_b: Ask the cause of the permitted evil in each of those effects — the fall, the long wasting, the final extinction — and I rightly name that person's drunkenness, blindness, and rashness. Ask the cause of my permission, or of my decree not to free him efficaciously, and you must come to the free power of my will, not to his ignorance or rashness. So God regards all men blind and wandering in sin's way: for some he prepares efficacious grace by which they shake off the stupor, return to themselves, and are saved; for others he decrees not to help with that powerful peculiar efficacious grace. Those latter rush into foul lusts, add sin to sin, harden in sin, die hardened, and are damned. Ask the cause of their rebellion, hardening, perdition: corrupt nature and voluntary sins are truly cause and origin of all those evils. Ask the cause of the permitting decree as to all that: you must come to the freest pleasure of the divine will, not to the permitted sins themselves. So the consequence wavers: sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore they also cause reprobation itself — the reprobating decree.

lemmas.gloss: cause of permission = free divine pleasure

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo: hardness is consequent event, not properly an effect of reprobation; Cajetan
latin: Secundo, videntur adversarii statuere in hoc argumento illam duritiem sive obdurationem, quae est mala dispositio aut perversa actio reprobati, esse effectum reprobationis Divinae. At hoc falsissimum est. Nam licet sit eventus consequens, non est tamen proprie dictum effectum reprobationis. Quamvis enim, ut bene notavit Cajetanus, quicquid ordinat praedestinatum ad vitam aeternam sit effectum praedestinationis, tamen in reprobatione est aliquid quod ordinat ad mortem (nimirum quicquid habet culpae aut peccati rationem, quale est praedicta obduratio et durities) quod est extra totum reprobationis effectum, In Aqu. 1. qu. 23. art. 5. Non enim (in quo nonnulli Theologi periculose errant) media et causae damnationis ita connexa sunt cum decreto reprobationis, sicuti media et causae salutis connectuntur cum decreto praedestinationis. Atque ratio discriminis in promptu est: Nam media et causae salutis sunt bona quaedam spiritualia; bonum autem subjacet providentiae Dei, ut intentum, causatum et ordinatum ab ea: sed media et causae quae ducunt ad damnationem sunt mala spiritualia; Malum autem hujusmodi subjacet Divinae providentiae, non ut intentum et causatum, sed ut praevisum, permissum, ordinatum. Sic Dionysius Carthusianus in 1. dist. 40. Quando ergo illa durities aut obduratio, quae est hominis vitium vel peccatum, supponitur effectus reprobationis, quod est merum consequens, effectus titulo improprie saltem, et non alio, insignitur.
pass_a: Secondly, the adversaries seem to establish in this argument that that hardness or hardening, which is the evil disposition or perverse action of the reprobated, is an effect of Divine reprobation. But this is most false. For although it is a consequent event, yet it is not properly said an effect of reprobation. For although, as Cajetan well noted, whatsoever ordains the predestined unto eternal life is an effect of predestination, yet in reprobation there is something that ordains unto death (namely whatsoever has the reason of fault or of sin, such as is the foresaid hardening and hardness) which is outside the whole effect of reprobation, On Aquinas 1, question 23, article 5. For (wherein some Theologians perilously err) the means and causes of damnation are not so connected with the decree of reprobation, as the means and causes of salvation are connected with the decree of predestination. And the reason of the discrimination is ready: For the means and causes of salvation are certain spiritual goods; but good is subject to the providence of God, as intended, caused, and ordained by it: but the means and causes which lead unto damnation are spiritual evils; But evil of this kind is subject to Divine providence, not as intended and caused, but as foresighted, permitted, ordained. So Dionysius the Carthusian on 1, distinction 40. When therefore that hardness or hardening, which is the vice or sin of man, is supposed an effect of reprobation, what is a mere consequent is marked with the title of effect improperly at least, and not otherwise.
pass_b: Second: adversaries seem to make that hardness or hardening — the reprobate's evil disposition or perverse act — an effect of divine reprobation. Most false. It may be a consequent event; it is not properly an effect of reprobation. As Cajetan well noted (on Aquinas I, q. 23 a. 5): whatever ordains the predestined to eternal life is an effect of predestination; yet in reprobation there is something that ordains to death — whatever has the character of fault or sin, such as that hardening and hardness — and that lies outside the whole effect of reprobation. Some theologians perilously err here: the means and causes of damnation are not tied to the reprobation decree as the means and causes of salvation are tied to the predestination decree. The difference is plain. Salvation's means are spiritual goods, and good falls under God's providence as intended, caused, and ordained by it. Damnation's means are spiritual evils; such evil falls under divine providence not as intended and caused, but as foresighted, permitted, ordained (so Dionysius the Carthusian on Sentences 1, dist. 40). When that hardness — man's vice or sin — is called an effect of reprobation, a mere consequent is labeled effect only improperly.

lemmas.gloss: damnation media not as salvation media

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo cont.: Rom. 1 / 2 Thess. / Pharaoh — further hardening vs first permissive denial
latin: Denique illa induratio, quam respicit Apostolus, Rom. i. 28, Quo spectant illa verba, Tradidit illos in reprobum sensum; item et illa quam 2 Thess. ii. 10, 11, 12, Apostolus hisce verbis depingit, Quia non receperunt amorem veritatis, propterea iis mittet Deus efficaciam deceptionis, ut credant mendacio, etc., non denotant negationem primae gratiae efficacis, qua posita talis obduratio nunquam evenisset, sed subductionem gratiae alicujus concessae, ex abusu ejusdem, quam subductionem fieri ex hominum demeritis non diffitemur: atque obdurationem inde consequentem et peccatum et peccati praecedentis mercedem agnoscimus. Quod autem de Pharaone dicitur Exod. ix. Obduravit Jehovah cor Pharaonis, id aut de prima negatione gratiae specialis, et permissiva obduratione intelligi debet, et tum haec voluntas obdurandi, id est, non-emolliendi, quae consideratur ut negatio gratuita actionis ex parte Dei, non potuit ex praevisis Pharaonis demeritis oriri, quia talem praevisionem antecedit. Hic igitur ad illud Apostoli confugiendum est, Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat. Vel possunt illa verba ad ulteriorem obdurationem referri, qua Pharao voluntaria pervicacia cor suum obfirmavit, Deo exterius et interius praebente illas occasiones, quibus certo praescivit Pharaonem magis obdurandum, etiamsi ex natura sua valere debuissent ad illum emolliendum. Deus igitur obdurat hominem impium propter sua demerita, quando ejus impietate provocatus sumit occasionem subducendi gratiam concessam, et quaedam agendi, ex quibus novit talem hominem fore deteriorem. Ac Deus etiam indurare dicitur absque hoc intuitu ad finalia demerita, ideo tantum quia vult, quando homini in communi massa considerato non praeparavit, non dedit illam specialem misericordiam, quam alteri in eadem misera conditione concessit. Atque haec est illa induratio quae arguit reprobationem, quaeque ex praevisione finalis perseverantiae in peccatis haud dependet. Ex aequivoco igitur non procedit argumentatio.
pass_a: Finally that hardening which the Apostle regards, Rom. 1:28, Whither those words look, He gave them over unto a reprobate mind; likewise also that which in 2 Thess. 2:10, 11, 12 the Apostle depicts with these words, Because they received not the love of the truth, therefore God shall send them the efficacy of deception, that they may believe a lie, etc., do not denote the negation of the first efficacious grace, which being posited such hardening would never have happened, but the subtraction of some grace granted, from the abuse of the same, which subtraction we do not deny to be made from the demerits of men: and we acknowledge the hardening thence consequent both as sin and as the wage of preceding sin. But what is said of Pharaoh Exod. 9. Jehovah hardened the heart of Pharaoh, that either ought to be understood of the first negation of special grace, and permissive hardening, and then this will of hardening, that is, of not-softening, which is considered as the gratuitous negation of an action on God's part, could not arise from the foresighted demerits of Pharaoh, because it precedes such foresight. Here therefore refuge must be taken unto that of the Apostle, He will have mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. Or those words can be referred unto a further hardening, by which Pharaoh by voluntary obstinacy stiffened his own heart, God outwardly and inwardly furnishing those occasions by which he certainly foresaw that Pharaoh would be more hardened, even if by their own nature they ought to have availed unto softening him. God therefore hardens an ungodly man on account of his demerits, when provoked by his impiety he takes occasion of subtracting granted grace, and of doing certain things from which he knows such a man will be worse. And God is also said to harden without this intuition unto final demerits, only because he wills, when to a man considered in the common mass he has not prepared, has not given that special mercy which he granted to another in the same miserable condition. And this is that hardening which argues reprobation, and which by no means depends from foresight of final perseverance in sins. From an equivocation therefore the argumentation does not proceed.
pass_b: Finally: the hardening Paul regards in Rom. 1:28 — He gave them over to a reprobate mind — and that which 2 Thess. 2:10-12 depicts — Because they received not the love of the truth, God shall send them strong delusion that they believe a lie — do not denote denial of the first efficacious grace, without which such hardening would never have come. They denote subtraction of some granted grace after its abuse — which subtraction we grant arises from men's demerits — and the hardening that follows we acknowledge as both sin and the wage of preceding sin. What is said of Pharaoh (Exod. 9: Jehovah hardened Pharaoh's heart) must either be taken of the first denial of special grace and permissive hardening — and then that will to harden, i.e. not to soften, as mere gratuitous negation of an act on God's part, could not arise from Pharaoh's foresighted demerits, because it precedes such foresight. Here refuge is Rom. 9: He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. Or those words may refer to a further hardening by which Pharaoh, of voluntary obstinacy, stiffened his own heart, God outwardly and inwardly furnishing occasions by which he certainly foresaw Pharaoh would be more hardened — even if by nature those occasions ought to have softened him. So God hardens an ungodly man for his demerits when, provoked by impiety, he takes occasion to withdraw granted grace and to act in ways he knows will make such a man worse. God is also said to harden without that regard to final demerits — only because he wills — when to a man considered in the common mass he has not prepared or given that special mercy he granted another in the same miserable condition. That is the hardening which argues reprobation, and it does not depend on foresight of final perseverance in sins. So the argument proceeds from an equivocation.

lemmas.gloss: Rom. 1 / 2 Thess.: further hardening after abuse
Pharaoh: first permissive denial precedes foresight
